correctness.rationale: The pair law changes by the signed kernel \((1,-2,1)\) times \(\delta\), so convolution gives the claimed point-mass second-difference identity and telescoping gives the CDF first-difference identity. For a Poisson-binomial background, the generating polynomial of the second-difference sequence is \((z-1)^2P(z)\), where the nonzero roots of \(P\) are real and nonpositive; the coefficient variation therefore has exactly two sign changes with positive ends. Unimodality then gives \(\sum_k|\Delta a_k|=2\max_k a_k\), yielding the Wasserstein formula, while total variation, Kolmogorov and stop-loss formulas follow directly from the same identities. Independent bounded checks on deterministic and nondegenerate backgrounds reproduced the two sign changes and the finite-difference identities.

value.rationale: A fixed-sum pair balancing move is the elementary step behind Bernoulli majorization. Quantifying that step simultaneously in the mass function, CDF, total variation, Kolmogorov distance, Wasserstein distance and stop-loss transform gives a compact structural transport lemma rather than an arbitrary numerical specialization. The exact two-crossing description sharpens the classical inequality direction and can be reused along majorization paths.
residual_risks: The identities are elementary once the pair-transfer kernel and Poisson-binomial shape facts are recognized.

limitations: The two-crossing and modal Wasserstein simplification require a Poisson-binomial background; the algebraic finite-difference identities do not.
Distances do not generally add over multiple balancing steps.
